claims.text: Rapid and nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors leads to synchronized nanoparticle nucleation.
Synchronized nucleation kinetically traps a homogeneous high-entropy alloy state.
Kinetic trapping prevents phase separation and elemental segregation.
A rapid thermal treatment or modified energy input can induce nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal precursors.
An inert or reducing atmosphere combined with a narrow temperature-time window enforces rapid kinetic control of precursor reduction.
The proposed treatment produces a transient, uniform nucleation stage in which all metal species are co-reduced and incorporated into forming nanoparticles.
Rapid synchronized reduction minimizes the time available for differential atomic mobility.
Minimizing the time available for differential atomic mobility suppresses phase segregation.
Forcing the constituent metals to nucleate and grow together traps the high-entropy state.
Rapid synchronous reduction will produce a more uniform elemental distribution than conventional asynchronous reduction.
Rapid synchronous reduction will produce a single-phase alloy structure more successfully than conventional asynchronous reduction.
Standard thermal treatments spread precursor reductions over a broader time window.
Standard thermal treatments typically result in phase separation, elemental segregation, or non-uniform morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems having relatively comparable reduction kinetics and miscibility.
The mechanism may fail when differences in reduction potentials or atomic mobilities are too large to be overcome by kinetic synchronization.
